issues.title: Replace concrete sentinel address with IPV4-SENTINEL (TBD1) throughout normative text
issues.author: remcovanmook
issues.body: Per AD guidance at IETF 126: normative text uses a symbolic name with a TBD placeholder. IANA Considerations requests one IPv4 address from 192.0.0.0/24 and suggests 192.0.0.11. Examples and figures move to 192.0.2.11 (RFC 5737 documentation space). Blocking for IESG review; do first in the WG -00.

issues.title: Section 5: router-to-host binding durability requirement (one paragraph)
issues.author: remcovanmook
issues.body: Add a single normative requirement: the first-hop router MUST maintain, for the lease lifetime, the ability to deliver to each /32 without depending on opportunistic neighbour-cache state. This prohibits the failure mode where an opportunistically learned MAC-to-IPv6 mapping is garbage collected and connectivity never recovers. Mechanisms stay out of this document (see companion draft issue). Raised in post-session design discussion.

issues.title: Section 5.3: ARP responder is operator-controlled migration machinery
issues.author: remcovanmook
issues.body: State explicitly that the router ARP responder exists for the migration period: enabled while unmodified hosts remain on the segment, disabled by the operator thereafter. A fully migrated segment is genuinely zero-ARP, responder included. Related design position: Section 4's MUST NOT stays strict; no host-side ARP fallback (a sanctioned fallback would make the responder unretirable from any segment, foreclosing the zero-ARP end state).

issues.title: Section 4: multi-homing exposition
issues.author: remcovanmook
issues.body: Adoption-call review (H. Robinson) showed the semantics are right but the exposition is poor. Explain the sentinel as an interface-scoped next-hop token; show the (prefix, interface, via-sentinel) route form; note that DHCPv4 already expresses this on both sides (per-interface Option 3 default plus Option 121 classless routes), demonstrated in the implementations repo; source selection follows the egress interface as today. Robinson's algorithm walkthrough in the call thread is raw material.

issues.title: Section 5: scope the ICMP redirect mention
issues.author: remcovanmook
issues.body: Redirects cannot express (destination, interface, sentinel) on multi-homed hosts, are operationally moribund, and are not needed: multi-router steering lives in RA preferences (RFC 4191). Rescope or remove the existing redirect sentence; state that redirects are not relied upon.

issues.title: Section 7: correct the off-link property basis (erratum from -01)
issues.author: remcovanmook
issues.body: The -01 Universal Gateway Address text derives off-link unreachability from Source=False; the correct basis is the Section 5.2 forwarding prohibition (the IANA table was always right: Source=True). Flagged at the IETF 126 session.

issues.title: Introduction: 'DHCPv4 configuration' -> 'DHCPv4 client configuration'
issues.author: remcovanmook
issues.body: From adoption-call review (H. Robinson).

issues.title: References: add pointer to the live IANA IPv4 Special-Purpose Address Registry
issues.author: remcovanmook
issues.body: Alongside the RFC 6890 citation. From adoption-call review (T. Petch).

issues.title: Introduction: add no-flag-day sentence
issues.author: remcovanmook
issues.body: Add: 'There is no flag day or mandatory switch-over point.' to close the incremental deployment argument.

issues.title: Introduction: OSS/BSS ecosystem argument for the sentinel
issues.author: remcovanmook
issues.body: A new DHCPv4 option requires changes across billing, provisioning, monitoring, NOC tooling and validation logic that encode the shape of an IPv4 gateway. The sentinel looks exactly like a valid gateway address to every existing system; the only place that needs to know is the host. Add to the alternatives discussion in the Introduction.

issues.title: Introduction rework: two-IPv4s framing and the layer cake
issues.author: remcovanmook
issues.body: Rework the Introduction around: (1) the internet-v4 vs local-network-v4 distinction (demand is off-link, architecture is on-link); (2) the dependency stack: subnet -> ARP -> FHRP -> carved pools -> IPv4 host, with the policing apparatus as side-stratum; (3) the demolition: /32 IS subnet deletion (what Hetzner/OVH/Scaleway did), sentinel deletes ARP's last job, FHRP loses its object, pools flatten; (4) precedents: RFC 3021 /31 lineage, VPN /32s (every OS runs subnet-less IPv4 on tunnel interfaces daily), 1982-isolation-assumption history (ARP designed alone on the wire, never revisited when IPv6 arrived). Segment tiering: access/hosting (no lateral v4), enterprise (auditable lateral v4, enclave-able), home WiFi (unauditable, out of scope). Candidate figure: before/after layer cake. See the published RIPE Labs articles for the worked prose.

issues.title: DC: ND operational-health prerequisites
issues.author: remcovanmook
issues.body: The mechanism inherits ND's operational prerequisites: icmp6 permitted on host firewalls, functioning MLD snooping / multicast forwarding, no MAC filtering of solicited-node groups. Already prerequisites for IPv6 service on the segment; state them explicitly. From list review.

issues.title: DC: east-west hairpinning cost and topology dependence
issues.author: remcovanmook
issues.body: The /32 model prices intra-segment IPv4 as a routed service. Cost is topology-dependent: on an L3 access switch the hairpinned path crosses the identical links as the switched path (zero extra wire cost, line rate); the double-traffic case is router-on-a-stick behind shared L2. Guidance: lead segments round to zero (lateral suppressed/absent or L3 access); genuinely east-west-heavy legacy shared-L2 segments should not opt in -- stay dual-stack or move that traffic to IPv6 first. From article review (A. Prado) with topology refinement from the adoption-call thread.

issues.title: DC: L2 integrity feature validation (snooping/DAI/IPSG)
issues.author: remcovanmook
issues.body: These features were written against subnet-and-binding assumptions; behaviour with an off-subnet gateway and /32 leases must be validated per platform. Textbook analysis: first-hop router sits on a DAI-trusted port, so the sentinel reply passes unchanged; host ARP requests validate against the sender binding (which the /32 lease provides); IPSG sees the leased address. Cover the residue: routers on untrusted ports, vendor variance on target/gratuitous-ARP inspection, bindings machinery beyond the classic trio. One static universal permit where needed. End state: apparatus unnecessary for IPv4 once the ARP tier is off. From article review (A. Prado).

issues.title: DC: new subsection 'Multiple gateways and redundancy'
issues.author: remcovanmook
issues.body: The sentinel behaves anycast-like where it counts (not anycast in the technical sense): resolved from the neighbour cache, never ARP-elected, so any number of routers can hold it with zero coordination; the requirement reduces to distinct IPv6 identities. Precision: this holds for the updated tier; unmodified hosts ARP and multiple routers answer last-reply-wins (benign nondeterminism; conventional FHRP remains available for the ARP tier where determinism is wanted). Every selectable router MUST forward IPv4 with an 8950 return path; steer via RFC 4191 where not all qualify. ECMP corollary: with correct route propagation every router originates each host /32, so return traffic is active-active by standard routing machinery; two independent healing planes (downstream at IGP convergence, upstream at RA/NUD pace). Caveat: stateful functions on segment routers inherit standard ECMP-asymmetry considerations. Explicit failover-MAC sentence: updated hosts elect nothing; unmodified hosts either accept re-ARP timing or run VRRP in front of the ARP tier. FHRP consumer taxonomy available for rationale: gateways and floating service VIPs are both 'an address that must appear on-link while its owner may change'; the /32 model moves the second to route origination (conditional origination from the active member for stateful pairs).

issues.title: DC: failover pacing, planned and unplanned
issues.author: remcovanmook
issues.body: IPv4 first-hop failover is paced by IPv6 default-router selection; no IPv4-specific latency. Planned decommission: final RA with Lifetime 0 (RFC 4861 s6.2.5) -- an operator requirement for RA daemon shutdown. Unplanned: NUD is traffic-driven; with active flows, DELAY/PROBE/FAILED and next-router selection in single-digit seconds (VRRP-default class); idle paths age out on lifetime by design; sub-second targets remain engineered (BFD class) exactly as with VRRP. Per-stack nuance: closed-platform realizations inherit the OS's NUD outcome. Note: DHCPv4 renew/release does not affect next-hop selection (empirically confirmed).

issues.title: Section 7: inspection collapse and FHRP attack surface
issues.author: remcovanmook
issues.body: (1) On a deployed segment the first-hop router is the only legitimate ARP responder; ARP inspection policy reduces to permitting replies solely from router ports, no snooping or per-host binding table required; host impersonation moves entirely to ND where RA Guard / ND inspection apply -- one protection stack for one resolution protocol. (2) Eliminating FHRP eliminates the FHRP attack surface: VRRP/HSRP spoofing and election manipulation cease to exist on sentinel segments.

issues.title: DC: reword the CLAT paragraph
issues.author: remcovanmook
issues.body: Make the demand-profile distinction explicit: CLAT provides outbound IPv4 via a shared PLAT pool (address sharing is the point); this mechanism provides a per-host routable IPv4 endpoint identity (per-host address is the point); not alternatives for the same host. Keep the claton interaction (CLAT disables when native IPv4 is available; the sentinel provides that trigger via ordinary DHCPv4). Drop or scope 'making CLAT unnecessary'. Optionally note the /32 need not be public: RFC 1918 /32s with edge NAT work unchanged on client segments. From list review.

issues.title: DC: access-provider base case (FTTH/DOCSIS/WiFi/FWA)
issues.author: remcovanmook
issues.body: Single public IPv4 per subscriber over an IPv6-only access network: no per-service-area carving, no gateway/broadcast overhead, no ARP at MAC-domain scale, flat pools (any /32 anywhere; nothing stranded by subnet sizing). Per-subscriber service differentiation falls out of the model: one segment serves public-IPv4, CGN-space and v6-only subscribers, distinguished purely in DHCP provisioning. Include FWA: same per-subscriber /32 story over the mobile operator's v6-only transport; converged operators get one v4-service architecture across FTTH, DOCSIS, WiFi and FWA, with 464XLAT remaining the handset answer.

issues.title: DC: DHCPv4 relay note
issues.author: remcovanmook
issues.body: Relaying interface needs no IPv4 address; giaddr requires a routable IPv4 address (one loopback per relay router suffices); RFC 3527 link-selection decouples giaddr from pool selection where needed; flat /32 pools largely dissolve pool selection (Option 82 circuit-id where segment identity is wanted). Cross-reference 192.0.0.8/32 (RFC 7600) for transit ICMPv4 sourcing alongside the 5.2 on-link sourcing. From article review.

issues.title: DC: return-path route origination, one informative sentence
issues.author: remcovanmook
issues.body: Note lease-triggered origination as existing practice: the first-hop router is (or snoops) the DHCPv4 relay, lease binding plus ND link-local, originates the RFC 8950 route, as BNGs do for subscriber routes today. Illustration only; route origination belongs to RFC 8950 / v4-via-v6 territory. Normative text unchanged.

issues.title: DC: return-path next-hop identity (stability under privacy addressing)
issues.author: remcovanmook
issues.body: Link-locals are shifting identifiers under modern privacy addressing (observed: dhcpcd moving EUI-64 to RFC 7217 mid-negotiation); return routes keyed to first-seen LL go stale during bring-up. Guidance: prefer a stable next-hop identity -- provider-known GUA, PD-anchored address, or SAVI/ND-snooping-derived binding (RFC 7513) -- with LL fallback; where only LLs are available, origination must track identity shifts via ND. Caveats: RFC 8981 temporaries rotate GUAs (servers keep use_tempaddr=0). Testbed mechanisms in the implementations repo (v4gw-lease.sh) demonstrate the GUA-preference and resolved-entries-only patterns.

issues.title: Related work: reinvention lineage note
issues.author: remcovanmook
issues.body: The pattern has been independently reinvented repeatedly: proxy ARP (RFC 925), 3GPP bearers, PPPoE/BRAS, the softwires IPv4aaS family (RFC 8585), container networking's static-ARP fake-gateway pattern (VERIFY Calico 169.254.1.1 details before citing), provider /32 hacks, route4via6. Each prior instance was blocked by a since-expired condition: no native transport (8950), unchangeable host stacks (Option 108/CLAT shipping disproved this), walled domains, transition orthodoxy. Position the draft as the first arrival after the blockers fell.

issues.title: Consider: alternatives-considered appendix
issues.author: remcovanmook
issues.body: Candidate appendix covering rejected designs with reasons: new DHCPv4 option (no coexistence tier; ecosystem shape change); IPv4 link-local next-hops (classic resolution keeps ARP; token variant collides with RFC 3927 self-assignment; per-router LLs reintroduce election); DHCPv6-PD-based IPv4 provisioning (restarts the client clock; IPv4 OSS/BSS learns DHCPv6); pure static / provider hacks (the gap itself). Status: under consideration, not committed.

issues.title: Companion informational draft: router-to-host configurations (skeleton)
issues.author: remcovanmook
issues.body: New informational I-D cataloguing acceptable router-to-host configurations under the Section 5 durability requirement: (a) lease-derived static entries in both directions; (b) lease-provoked ND (construct-and-ping the host GUA from DHCP state); (c) orchestrated / route-reflector-fed; (d) PD-anchored identity. Plus per-segment-type recipes (datacenter, access/BNG, enterprise), the dnsmasq/testbed configuration appendix, and conditional-origination patterns for stateful service pairs. All core mechanisms already implemented in the implementations repo. First task: title, abstract, section skeleton.

issues.title: Post-adoption: RFC 7120 early allocation request
issues.author: remcovanmook
issues.body: File for early allocation of the sentinel address (requires WG adoption, chairs, AD approval) so the code point is assigned ahead of IESG review and deployed implementations stay aligned with the registry. Raise with the chairs when the adoption call concludes.

issues.author: remcovanmook
issues.body: Track draft-palet-v6ops-ipv6-only for IPv6-Only-Strict terminology; align our segment terminology if it advances.

issues.author: remcovanmook
issues.body: Could be an informational companion or a short chapter in this draft - previously left out in the assumption that v4-via-v6 would clear all of that.

issues.title: Abstract: state the DHCPv4 provisioning step explicitly
issues.author: remcovanmook
issues.body: Abstract currently implies provisioning ('Hosts that receive...'); make the two steps explicit: hosts are provisioned through ordinary, unmodified DHCPv4 (typically; static config also in scope), and the sentinel value changes only the resolution step. From article review (H. Kramselund).

pulls.title: fix: skip tag-annotation fetch step on workflow_dispatch
pulls.author: remcovanmook
pulls.body:
The 'Get Tag Annotations' step runs:
  git fetch -f origin ${{ github.ref }}:${{ github.ref }}

When the workflow is triggered manually (workflow_dispatch), github.ref resolves to refs/heads/main. Git refuses to fetch into a branch that is already checked out, exiting with code 128.

The fetch is only meaningful for tag-triggered runs (it retrieves annotated tag metadata that the shallow checkout misses). Add an 'if: startsWith(github.ref, "refs/tags/")' condition so the step is skipped entirely on manual dispatch triggers.

pulls.title: Use symbolic IPV4-SENTINEL (TBD1) in normative text
pulls.author: remcovanmook
pulls.body:
Per AD guidance at IETF 126: normative text uses a symbolic name with a TBD placeholder, so no concrete value is baked in ahead of the IANA assignment. Flagged in #2 as blocking for IESG review and to be done first in the WG -00.

## What changed

- **Conventions** now defines `IPV4-SENTINEL`, carries an RFC Editor replacement note, and states that examples use `192.0.2.11` from TEST-NET-1 (RFC 5737).
- **Normative text, pseudocode and prose**: all prose and pseudocode occurrences of `192.0.0.11` become `IPV4-SENTINEL`.
- **IANA Considerations** is the only place a concrete value appears: it requests one address from the 192.0.0.0/24 IETF Protocol Assignments block and suggests `192.0.0.11/32`. The Address Block row reads `TBD1 (suggested: 192.0.0.11/32)`.
- **Packet-flow figure** now shows the host IPv4 gateway as `192.0.2.11`, so the documentation-range convention is actually exercised rather than just asserted.
- RFC 5737 citation normalised to header-declared form (silences a kramdown-rfc duplicate-reference warning).

The IANA table `Source = True` is left alone - #7 confirms the table was always right, and correcting the Section 7 prose that contradicts it is that issue's job.

Closes #2

pulls.title: Abstract: separate provisioning from resolution
pulls.author: remcovanmook
pulls.body:
The abstract implied the provisioning step rather than stating it - "Hosts that receive `192.0.0.11/32` as their IPv4 default gateway address resolve..." leaves the reader to work out whether new DHCPv4 machinery is involved.

Now the two steps are separate and explicit:

1. **Provisioning is unchanged** - the host obtains its IPv4 address and default gateway through ordinary, unmodified DHCPv4, or by static configuration. Static config is named, since it is in scope.
2. **Only the gateway value changes** - when that value is the sentinel, next-hop resolution comes from the IPv6 neighbor cache instead of ARP, and nothing else about IPv4 operation is altered.

From article review (H. Kramselund).

Closes #30

pulls.title: Introduction: adoption-call review items and Related Work
pulls.author: remcovanmook
pulls.body:
Four of the five Introduction issues. **#12 (the two-IPv4s framing and layer cake rework) is deliberately not here** - it is waiting on the two RIPE Labs article links, and it will reshape the section around what is added below rather than conflict with it.

## Commits

- **#8** - `DHCPv4 configuration` -> `DHCPv4 client configuration`. The original was ambiguous between client and server side; the verified result is specifically that no client configuration changes are needed. (H. Robinson)
- **#10** - closes the incremental-deployment argument: the two tiers coexist indefinitely, conversion is per host, and there is no flag day or mandatory switch-over point.
- **#11** - the OSS/BSS argument for the sentinel. The alternatives discussion previously counted only host stack changes; the larger cost of a new DHCPv4 option lands in billing, provisioning, inventory, monitoring, NOC tooling and validation logic, all of which encode the shape of an IPv4 gateway. A sentinel is indistinguishable from an ordinary gateway address to every one of them.
- **#24** - a new `1.1 Related Work` subsection covering the reinvention lineage (proxy ARP, PPPoE/3GPP bearers, softwires IPv4aaS, Calico, provider /32s, pre-standard v4-via-v6), then the blocking conditions that have since expired, positioning the draft as the first general and interoperable arrival.

## On the Calico citation

The issue said to verify before citing. Confirmed against the current Project Calico FAQ: `169.254.1.1` is never assigned to any interface and is resolved solely by `proxy_arp` on the host side of the veth pair - the container's routing table sends everything via it, so it is the only address the workload ever ARPs. The draft text reflects exactly that and claims nothing more.

Worth noting for #25: Calico's IPv6 side uses a real link-local resolved by ordinary NDP, and needs no equivalent hack. That is the same asymmetry this draft is closing, and it is useful supporting material if the alternatives-considered appendix goes ahead.

New informative references: RFC 925, RFC 2516, RFC 8585, CALICO-FAQ. Build is clean and all five resolve.

Closes #8, closes #10, closes #11, closes #24

pulls.title: Section 4: expand the multi-homing exposition
pulls.author: remcovanmook
pulls.body:
Adoption-call review (H. Robinson) found the multi-homing semantics correct but the exposition poor - it was one sentence. This gives it a `4.1 Multi-Homed Hosts` subsection.

## What the exposition now says

- **The sentinel is an interface-scoped next-hop token**, not the address of a particular router. It denotes "the IPv6 default router on this interface" and carries no topological information, so the same value on two interfaces resolves to two different link-layer addresses via two different default router lists. The IPv6 link-local next-hop analogy is made explicit, since that is the property being reused.
- **The route form is a triple**, `(destination prefix, outgoing interface, via IPV4-SENTINEL)`, shown alongside the two-interface case so it is visible that two sentinel default routes are two distinct routes and not a conflict. They disambiguate by outgoing interface and by the host's existing default-route metric or policy.
- **DHCPv4 already expresses this on both sides** - per-interface Option 3 default from the lease, and Option 121 (RFC 3442) for more specific routes, whose router field takes the sentinel like any other next-hop. No extension needed.
- **Source selection follows the egress interface** as today, and the sentinel is never a candidate source address.

The normative `MUST NOT` on cross-interface resolution is unchanged in wording; it moves to open the new subsection rather than sitting mid-section before the pseudocode.

New informative reference RFC 3442. Anchors added to 5.2 and Section 8 so the new cross-references resolve.

Closes #5

pulls.title: Section 5: redirects, binding durability, ARP responder lifecycle
pulls.author: remcovanmook
pulls.body:
The three Section 5 issues, one commit each.

## #6 - scope out ICMPv4 redirects

The old sentence offered redirects as the route to host-to-host IPv4 on the segment. They cannot carry the `(destination, interface, sentinel)` form that next-hop resolution takes here, so on a multi-homed host a redirect is ambiguous, and they are widely filtered or ignored in practice. The text now states plainly that the mechanism does not rely on them, and points multi-router steering at RFC 4191 Default Router Preference - which is per interface and already required for router selection, so nothing new is introduced.

## #3 - router-to-host binding durability (new 5.2, normative)

> A first-hop router MUST be able, for the lifetime of a host's IPv4 address assignment, to deliver IPv4 traffic to that host's /32 without depending on opportunistically learned neighbor cache state.

The failure mode is spelled out because it is not obvious and it is unrecoverable: if the /32 route derives from a neighbor cache entry learned only as a side effect of traffic, garbage collection of that entry withdraws the route, and the inbound traffic that would provoke re-resolution is then dropped upstream for want of a route. Nothing restores it. The host cannot detect or repair the condition, because it has no way to learn it has become unreachable from outside - an idle host stays unreachable indefinitely.

Mechanisms stay out of the document per the issue. The closing paragraph names the shape of acceptable answers (lease-derived binding, lease-provoked ND, orchestrated distribution, PD anchoring) and defers the catalogue to the companion draft.

## #4 - ARP responder is migration machinery (5.4)

The responder read as a permanent property of the router. It is now explicitly operator-controlled and transitional: SHOULD be enabled while unmodified hosts remain, SHOULD be disabled once none do, and a fully migrated segment exchanges no ARP at all, responder included.

The second paragraph records the design position behind the strict host-side `MUST NOT` rather than leaving it implicit: a sanctioned ARP fallback would make the responder unretirable from *any* segment, since a conformant host might fall back at any time. That permanently forecloses the zero-ARP end state, in exchange for masking a misconfiguration better surfaced.

## Cross-references

Inserting 5.2 renumbers the two subsections after it, so the four hardcoded `Section 4` / `Section 5.2` / `Section 5.3` mentions are converted to anchors. They now resolve automatically and cannot go stale on the next insertion. Verified in the built text.

Closes #6, closes #3, closes #4

pulls.title: Deployment Considerations: structure, applicability, prerequisites
pulls.author: remcovanmook
pulls.body:
First of three Deployment Considerations PRs (per the agreed split). This one carries the structural work, so the other two land cleanly on top of it.

## Structure

Section 6 was a flat run of paragraphs in no particular order, and the adoption call roughly triples it. The first commit introduces subsections and moves exactly one paragraph ("hosts without functional IPv6") up under Applicability. No prose changes in that commit.

Three paragraphs are parked in `6.x Host Implementation Considerations` for now - equal-DRP router selection, the IPC note, and relay gateway validation. The next two PRs relocate the first into *Multiple gateways and redundancy* and the third into *Return path*.

## Issues

**#19 - CLAT paragraph.** "Making CLAT unnecessary" overreached and framed CLAT as competing for the same job. The distinction is demand profile: CLAT gives outbound IPv4 through a pool shared at the PLAT, where address sharing is the point and the host has no address a remote peer can reach; this mechanism gives a per-host end-to-end routable identity with inbound reachability. Not alternatives for the same host. The claton interaction is kept intact, and the note that the /32 need not be public (RFC 1918 plus edge NAT) is added.

**#20 - access-provider base case.** The case that motivates the work was never actually stated. Now covers what the /32 model removes (per-service-area carving, subnet/broadcast overhead, stranding by subnet sizing, ARP at MAC-domain scale), the flat pool, per-subscriber differentiation falling out of DHCPv4 provisioning alone, and FTTH/DOCSIS/wireless/FWA convergence with 464XLAT left as the handset answer.

**#13 - ND prerequisites.** ICMPv6 permitted on host firewalls, working multicast/MLD snooping, no filtering of solicited-node groups. All already prerequisites for IPv6 on the segment; stated because an operator whose ND health has never been examined will otherwise meet the dependency as an IPv4 symptom.

**#14 - east-west hairpinning.** The "double the traffic" objection is topology-dependent and usually overstated. On an L3 access switch or leaf the hairpinned path crosses the identical links at line rate - a forwarding lookup, not extra wire. The real double-bandwidth case is router-on-a-stick behind shared L2. Guidance is by demand: access/hosting rounds to zero, L3 access is a lookup, and a genuinely east-west-heavy shared-L2 segment should not adopt this first.

**#15 - L2 integrity features.** Validation needed per platform, then the textbook analysis (trusted router port, sender binding from the /32 lease, IPSG sees the leased address), then the residue that the analysis does not cover: untrusted router ports, vendor variance on target and gratuitous ARP inspection, binding machinery beyond the classic trio. One universal static permit suffices where needed, since the sentinel is the same value on every segment.

New informative references: RFC 1918, RFC 6877.

Closes #19, closes #20, closes #13, closes #14, closes #15

pulls.title: Deployment Considerations: redundancy and failover pacing
pulls.author: remcovanmook
pulls.body:
Second of three Deployment Considerations PRs. Two new subsections, `6.7 Multiple Gateways and Redundancy` and `6.8 First-Hop Failover Pacing`.

## #16 - Multiple gateways and redundancy

The central point: because the sentinel is resolved from the neighbour cache and never ARP-elected, any number of routers can present it with zero coordination and no shared virtual address. The requirement collapses to *distinct IPv6 identities*, which routers need anyway. The text calls this anycast-like in effect while stating plainly that it is not anycast in the technical sense.

The precision from the issue is kept rather than smoothed away:

- It holds for the **updated tier only**. Unmodified hosts ARP, and multiple answering routers give last-reply-wins - benign, since every answerer is a valid first hop, but nondeterministic. Conventional FHRP remains available in front of the ARP tier where determinism is wanted.
- **Normative**: every selectable router MUST forward the host's IPv4 and MUST have an RFC 8950 return path; where not all qualify, operators MUST steer with RFC 4191 preference.
- **ECMP corollary**: with correct origination every router originates each host /32, so return traffic is active-active through standard routing machinery, with two independently healing planes (downstream at routing convergence, upstream at RA/NUD pace). The stateful-function ECMP-asymmetry caveat is noted.
- **No failover MAC**: updated hosts elect and inherit nothing; unmodified hosts either accept re-ARP timing or sit behind VRRP.
- Closes with the FHRP consumer taxonomy - gateway addresses and floating service VIPs are the same requirement, "an address that must appear on-link while its owner may change" - and notes that the /32 model moves the second to route origination, conditionally from the active member for stateful pairs.

The equal-preference/ECMP-fabric paragraph moves here from the host implementation notes, where it had been parked.

## #17 - First-hop failover pacing

Leads with the answer operators actually want: failover is paced by IPv6 default-router selection, with no IPv4-specific detection and no IPv4-specific latency.

- **Planned** - final RA with Router Lifetime 0 (RFC 4861 §6.2.5) removes the router on receipt, so no detection is involved. Stated as an operator requirement for RA daemon shutdown, with the consequence of omitting it named: the planned change degrades into the unplanned case.
- **Unplanned** - NUD is traffic-driven. Active flows give DELAY/PROBE/FAILED and reselection in single-digit seconds (VRRP-default class); idle paths detect nothing by design and age out on lifetime; sub-second targets stay engineered (BFD, shortened RA intervals) exactly as with VRRP.
- Two nuances recorded: separate-stack platforms inherit the OS's NUD outcome, and DHCPv4 renew/release does not affect next-hop selection.

On that last point - the issue notes it was empirically confirmed. The draft states the behaviour as fact without claiming test evidence, since the test itself is not in the document; say the word if you would rather it cite the implementations repo.

Closes #16, closes #17

pulls.title: Deployment Considerations: return path and DHCPv4 relay
pulls.author: remcovanmook
pulls.body:
Last of the three Deployment Considerations PRs. Two new subsections, `6.9 Return Path Provisioning` and `6.10 DHCPv4 Relay Considerations`.

## #22 - lease-triggered origination

One informative paragraph, as the issue specifies. Where the first-hop router is the DHCPv4 relay or snoops relayed traffic, it already holds the lease binding; with the host's link-layer address from ND that is enough to originate the RFC 8950 route at lease grant and withdraw it at lease end - which is what BNGs do for subscriber routes today. Marked as illustration only, with route origination left to RFC 8950 and v4-via-v6. No normative text.

## #23 - next-hop identity stability

The failure this prevents is subtle and bites during bring-up: an implementation that moves from an interface-identifier-derived link-local to an RFC 7217 opaque one can do so *mid-DHCPv4-exchange*, so a return route keyed to the first link-local observed is stale before the host has finished configuring.

Guidance is to key return routes to a stable identity where one exists - a provider-known GUA, a PD-anchored address, or an ND-snooping/SAVI-derived binding (RFC 7513) - with link-local as fallback, and to track identity shifts through ND where only link-locals are available.

One wording call worth flagging: the issue notes RFC 8981 temporaries rotate, with the parenthetical that servers keep `use_tempaddr=0`. I wrote that as a `MUST NOT` on temporary addresses as next-hop identity and left the Linux sysctl out, since it is platform-specific detail that dates quickly in an RFC. Easy to soften to a SHOULD if you think MUST overreaches for a Deployment Considerations section.

## #21 - DHCPv4 relay

- Relaying interface needs no IPv4 address; giaddr does need a routable one, but one loopback per relay router covers any number of segments.
- RFC 3527 link selection decouples giaddr from pool selection where they would be conflated - though flat /32 pools largely dissolve the question, with Option 82 circuit-id (RFC 3046) carrying segment identity where it is still wanted.
- RFC 7600 and `192.0.0.8/32` cross-referenced for ICMPv4 sourced by IPv6-only transit routers, set against the interface-local sentinel sourcing in 5.3.

The existing on-link gateway validation paragraph moves here from the host implementation notes.

New informative references: RFC 3046, RFC 3527, RFC 7217, RFC 7513, RFC 8981.

With this merged, `6.11 Host Implementation Considerations` is back to the single paragraph it should always have been (the separate-stack IPC note); everything else parked there has found its home.

Closes #22, closes #23, closes #21

pulls.title: Security Considerations: off-link basis erratum, inspection collapse, FHRP surface
pulls.author: remcovanmook
pulls.body:
The two Security Considerations issues.

## #7 - off-link property basis (erratum from -01)

The -01 text derived off-link unreachability from "Source=False in the IANA registry". The registry entry says **Source=True**, and always has, so the stated basis contradicted the table it cited in the same sentence.

The correct basis is the forwarding prohibition in 5.3 - the sentinel MUST NOT appear as source or destination in any forwarded packet - which confines it to the segment in both directions with no appeal to the Source field at all.

Rather than just deleting the wrong clause, the text now says why Source=True is right: a first-hop router *does* legitimately originate interface-local ICMPv4 with the sentinel as source. What confines the address is that no such message is ever forwarded. That should stop the same correction being proposed again by the next reviewer who checks the table against the prose.

No change to the IANA table, which was right all along.

## #18 - inspection collapse and FHRP surface

**Inspection collapse** (added to 7.1): on a deployed segment the first-hop router is the only legitimate ARP responder, and the sentinel is the only address it answers for, so ARP inspection policy reduces to "permit ARP replies from router ports, deny elsewhere". That needs no snooping database and no per-host binding table, because the policy never refers to host addresses. Host impersonation is not eliminated but relocated - entirely to ND, where RA Guard and ND inspection already apply. One protection stack for one resolution protocol, instead of parallel ARP and ND stacks kept consistent by hand.

**FHRP attack surface** (new 7.2): where redundancy no longer needs an FHRP, VRRP/HSRP advertisement spoofing and election manipulation do not become *mitigated* - they become impossible, since no election takes place. Stated with its condition attached: an operator keeping conventional FHRP in front of the ARP tier keeps the surface for as long as it runs. Worth being explicit about, because this is the kind of claim that otherwise gets quoted without its precondition.

Closes #7, closes #18

pulls.title: Introduction: two-IPv4s framing, dependency stack, segment tiering
pulls.author: remcovanmook
pulls.body:
The Introduction rework, built from the worked prose in [A Farewell to ARPs](https://labs.ripe.net/author/remco-van-mook/a-farewell-to-arps-ipv4-service-on-ipv6-only-networks/) and [What's ARP Got To Do With It](https://labs.ripe.net/author/remco-van-mook/whats-arp-got-to-do-with-it/). Last of the wg-00 document issues.

The Introduction used to open with the mechanism, leaving the argument for it implicit. It now makes the architectural case first and arrives at the mechanism as a consequence.

## 1.1 Two Kinds of IPv4

The central separation: the IPv4 applications require is reachability past the first hop, where demand is real and durable; the IPv4 networks deploy to satisfy it is subnet, broadcast domain, ARP and an on-link gateway, which no application asks for. Needing to reach IPv4 has been taken to entail being attached to an IPv4 network, and that conflation is the document's actual subject.

Then the observation that on access and hosting segments the local part was never used - lateral traffic is suppressed by design, so the only on-link destination ever resolved is the gateway - and RFC 3021 as the standing precedent that a subnet may contain nothing but the ends of a link. The netmask as compression scheme, ARP as decompressor.

## 1.2 The Local IPv4 Dependency Stack

subnet → ARP → FHRP → carved pools → IPv4 host, with the policing apparatus (snooping, DAI, binding tables) as a side stratum rather than a layer, since it exists only because the base is an unauthenticated broadcast feeding a single-answer table. Includes the before/after layer cake figure.

Closes on the history: ARP was specified in 1982 on the assumption it was alone on the wire, which was true at the time. What did not follow was revision - IPv6 arrived on the same links with a complete resolution service and IPv4 resolution was never reconsidered, the dual-stack model holding the two deliberately independent.

## 1.3 Removing the Base Layer

The demolition in order: /32 *is* subnet deletion and Hetzner/OVH/Scaleway have shipped it for years (each with a different address and per-OS recipe, in no RFC); the sentinel deletes ARP's last remaining job; FHRP loses its object, since there is no longer an address to elect an owner for; pools go flat; policing collapses to one rule.

Ends on the precedent that lands best with sceptics: every mainstream OS already runs subnet-less IPv4 on tunnel interfaces daily, closed platforms included. What changes is not whether a host *can* work this way, but how it is told to.

## 1.4 The Mechanism

The former opening material, now arriving after the case for it. Content from #8, #10 and #11 is preserved intact.

## 6.1 Applicability - segment tiering

The tiering the issue lists went here rather than into the Introduction, since 6.1 previously said only that hosts without IPv6 are out of scope, and this is applicability. The test is the one 1.1 sets up - does lateral IPv4 exist, and can it be enumerated:

- **Access and hosting** - clearest case, removing the subnet costs nothing that was in use.
- **Enterprise and campus** - managed estate, on-link IPv4 can be inventoried; IPv4-only remnants are already statically administered and can be enclaved.
- **Residential** - out of scope, unauditable local-IPv4 assumptions and hosts that genuinely do address each other.
- **IXP peering LANs** - out of scope, from the second article. No default gateway, every destination a peer, all traffic lateral by design. A mechanism for resolving the way *off* a segment has nothing to offer one that is nothing but exits. Worth having explicitly, since it is the obvious "what about..." from the room.

New informative reference: RFC 3021.

One note on register: the articles argue conversationally and the draft cannot, so the arguments and analogies carry over but the voice does not. If any of it reads as too polemical for a standards-track Introduction, the layer-cake material in 1.2 is the most compressible.

Closes #12

- **#30** — the abstract states the provisioning step: ordinary DHCPv4 or static configuration, with the gateway value the only change.
- **#8** — "DHCPv4 configuration" → "DHCPv4 client configuration".
- **#9** — cites the live IANA registry alongside RFC 6890.

`192.0.0.11/32` is currently unassigned in the registry.
